paragraphs.heading: Resistance to flowing
paragraphs.text: Viscosity measures how much a fluid resists when one part of it moves relative to another. For a liquid it matches the everyday idea of thickness: syrup has a higher viscosity than water. In liquids it comes from cohesive forces between molecules, while in gases it comes from molecules colliding. Apart from superfluids, every fluid has some viscosity, so every flow feels its effects to some degree.

paragraphs.heading: Pushing fluid through a tube
paragraphs.text: Force a viscous fluid such as syrup through a tube and it moves faster along the middle than near the walls. To keep it flowing you need a steady push, such as a pressure difference between the two ends. That push is needed to overcome friction between layers of fluid moving at different speeds. For a steady flow rate, the push grows in proportion to the fluid's viscosity.

paragraphs.heading: Two sliding plates
paragraphs.text: A simple picture, called Couette flow, traps fluid between two huge flat plates. The bottom plate stays still and the top one slides at a constant speed. If it moves slowly enough to avoid turbulence, the fluid moves in layers, from standing still at the bottom to the plate's speed at the top. Each layer rubs against the one below, so the fluid drags back on the moving plate, and an outside force is needed to keep it going.

paragraphs.heading: Speed, not distance
paragraphs.text: This is what sets viscosity apart from springiness. A spring pushes back in proportion to how far it has been moved, and stresses tied to that kind of shape change are called elastic. In water, the stress from shearing does not depend on how far the fluid has been sheared but on how quickly. Stresses tied to the rate of deformation are called viscous, and viscosity is the property that links them to that rate.

paragraphs.heading: Units and symbols
paragraphs.text: Scientifically, viscosity is a force multiplied by a time and divided by an area. Its SI unit is therefore the pascal-second, which is the same as a newton-second per square metre. Engineers, mathematicians and physicists often write it with the Greek letter mu (μ). Chemists and the IUPAC also use the letter eta (η).

paragraphs.heading: What changes it
paragraphs.text: In general, a fluid's viscosity depends on its temperature, its pressure and how fast it is being deformed. For a Newtonian fluid, the speed of deformation makes little difference. Zero viscosity is seen only in superfluids at very low temperatures; otherwise the second law of thermodynamics requires viscosity to be positive. The word comes from the Latin viscum, mistletoe, which also named a sticky glue made from mistletoe berries.
